findings: The frozen repository context contains three equivalent JVM memory-area questions and explicitly requests heap, JVM stack, method area and program-counter coverage. The candidate answers all three source variants directly and preserves the requested scope before mentioning adjacent JVM areas.

The Java SE 26 JVMS primary-source packet supports the central sharing and lifetime model used in the answer: heap and method area are JVM-wide shared areas, while each thread has its own JVM stack and pc register; the per-thread areas follow thread lifetime.

The stack/frame explanation is source-aligned and avoids the common category error that a local variable holding a reference means the referenced object is itself stored in the JVM stack. It correctly distinguishes the per-thread JVM stack from frames created for method invocations and covers local variables, operand stack and linking/return support.

The heap section is appropriately specification-bounded: class instances and arrays are allocated from the JVMS heap abstraction, storage is reclaimed by automatic storage management, and neither a specific collector nor physically contiguous heap memory is presented as a JVM requirement.

The method-area section preserves the most important implementation boundary. It treats Method Area as a JVMS abstraction for per-class structures, including the run-time constant pool, and does not universally equate it with HotSpot Metaspace or historical PermGen. It also keeps the JVMS logical-part-of-heap wording separate from physical placement claims.

The pc-register and failure-boundary material is source-supported: pc is per-thread, a non-native current method has a JVM instruction address, a native current method leaves the pc value undefined, JVM-stack depth can produce StackOverflowError, and relevant allocation failures can produce OutOfMemoryError.

The candidate does not fabricate a production OOM incident, JVM sizing number or GC result. Its project section is framed as a diagnostic mapping procedure rather than claimed personal history. The one-minute answer is compact enough for practical recall; the three-minute section is substantially longer than literal oral timing, so oral quality is scored 4/5.
